title: Can't you stop yawning? It could be a hidden sign that has a serious lung problem: Dr. Ellie
text:
I am 84 years old and I can’t stop yawning. He is bothering my family and friends because they think I’m bored of them. I am not tired either, so that cannot be the cause. What do I have to do?
Dr. Ellie Cannon replies: Excessive yawn can be a sign of a breathing problem.
The breathing is controlled by the muscles of the chest wall and the diaphragm, a large muscle under the lungs.
Most of us really do not think about how we breathe, unless we are singing or exercising, because it is something we do automatically. However, some people can develop a problem called dysfunctional breathing, where the rhythm is interrupted or inefficient.
Yawn is a symptom, along with difficulty breathing or persistent cough.
In general, it is triggered by lung problems such as asthma.
Dr. Ellie helps a patient worried about her excessive yawn
Dysfunctional breathing is also a reported effect of long and persistent symptoms that can last weeks, even months, after an infection with the virus.
A header can send patients with a dysfunctional breathing to a respiratory physiotherapist, which should help handle the condition and correct breathing so that yawn occurs less frequently.
The header should also evaluate what, if something, is causing the problem. For example, asthma, which can be handled with inhalers.
Treating the underlying condition must also relieve part of the yawn.
I have suffered with low and pelvic back pain for years, and I also need to urinate about five times every night. I am 78 years old. What could be wrong?
Dr. Ellie Cannon replies: Lumbar pain is one of the most common health complaints, particularly among older people.
For some, this pain will be resolved without treatment after a few months. However, if an elderly patient suffers from severe back pain and pelvic who is waking them at night, it is likely that he should refer to the hospital to obtain scan, because these can be a sign of a serious problem in the spine .
This could be arthritis, which occurs when the bones of the column are damaged and the nerves are crushed, causing severe pain.
However, it can also be a sign of the osteoporosis of the bone disease. This condition, which is more common in women, causes bones to crumble and increase the risk of dangerous fractures.
That is why it is so urgent that older patients with these symptoms are seen in the hospital. There are medications that can be given to reduce the risk of serious fractures.
Less frequently, lower back can be a sign of certain cancers, for example, myeloma, which affects the bone marrow.
If an older woman complains of pelvic pain, then she would probably need to have a pelvic exploration to rule out the possibility of ovarian cancer. This disease can also trigger changes in urinary habits. Therefore, it is crucial that anyone who has a severe back later in life makes an appointment with their header.
Recently I had a mini stroke that made my left arm stir without control. Apparently I suffered a brain bleeding that caused an epileptic event on my arm. Now I am taking medications and I am for a check with my neurologist in a month. Am I allowed to drive before that?
Dr. Ellie Cannon replies: After a mini stroke, it is assumed that patients should not drive a car or a motorcycle for at least a month.
A mini stroke, also known as a transient ischemic attack, occurs when blood flow in the brain is temporarily blocked. In some cases, patients experience few symptoms. On the contrary, a stroke is a more durable block that can lead to long -term disability.
A mini stroke can lead to deteriorated mental function or alter the normal function of other parts of the body, for example, limb movement.
For this reason, patients have the legal duty to inform the driver and vehicle licenses agency (DVLA) about a mini recent stroke or stroke.
It depends on the DVLA, not to the NHS, when it is certain that patients will drive again after one of these health events.
The DVLA also has separate regulations for epilepsy and seizures that can affect patients with stroke.
For example, if a stroke triggers an epileptic event, and there are reasons to believe that the same could happen again, patients can be excluded
from driving for six months. However, if a doctor decides that it is unlikely that the patient experiences another epileptic event in the near future, a month prohibition may be sufficient.
This decision would be based on a neurologist’s decision, so patients should not drive until they attended this event.
The DVLA guide on health conditions can be found in detail on its website (GOV.UK).

I was moved to listen to Thomas Kingston’s parents to speak for the first time last week about his premature death.
Lady Gabriella Windsor’s husband, 45, took his life last year after suffering ‘adverse effects’ triggered by new antidepressants he had been taking, according to a coroner.
Thomas had been using the Serstraline drug before his header changed it to another tablet called Citalopram. Both are called selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRs) and, in some rare cases, moodid changes or suicidal thoughts can trigger.
It is for this reason I always advise my patients to tell their family and friends when they begin to take SSRS.
Loved ones must take into account the agitation or worsening of mood. If these symptoms occur, the patient should be seen by his header as quickly as possible or go to A & e immediately. This is so crucial that if a patient tells me that he does not intend to tell anyone about his new medicine, I often do not prescribe it.
Did the warning of prediabetes work? I was surprised to read that the American medical expert who coined the term prediabetes now believes that he made “a big mistake.”
Dr. Richard Kahn, formerly from the American Diabetes Association, reached the term in 2001.
The intention was to warn patients who were on the way to developing type 2 diabetes, the condition of blood sugar that affects more than four million in the United Kingdom.
Patients are diagnosed with prediabetes if their blood sugar is constantly raised but not high enough to be diabetic.
Dr. Kahn now believes that the diagnosis of patients with prediabetes has not reduced diabetes cases while covering the pockets of pharmaceutical companies that manufacture medications to reduce blood sugar.
However, I do not agree. I find that when I tell people in my surgery that are prediabetic, they are more likely to improve their diet and lifestyle, which reduces their risk of full -fledged diabetes.
Have you been told that you are prediabetic? Was it useful? Please write and make it know.
